content: Boxthorn, scientifically known as Lycium, is a genus within the tribe Lycieae and the family Solanaceae. It comprises approximately 90 species of plants that are predominantly distributed across subtropical regions worldwide. These plants are typically found in arid, semi-saline environments. Common names for Lycium species include wolfberry, desert-thorn, Christmas berry, Matrimony vine, and the misleading Tea-tree (which is unrelated to actual tea and should not be consumed as such due to the toxicity of its foliage). The term goji has become a popular English name, largely due to the marketing of certain juices and dried berries in the United States, often branded as Tibetan or Himalayan goji berries, though these labels do not accurately reflect the geographical origins of the fruit. The genus Lycium is represented by approximately 20 species in North America, 30 species in South America, 30 species in Africa, 10 species in Eurasia, and one species in Australia. The genera Grabowskia and Phrodus are closely related to Lycium and are also part of the tribe Lycieae. Plants in the Lycium genus are long-lived, perennial, thorny shrubs. They have deciduous, alternate, simple leaves that range from 1 to 8 cm in length. The flowers are either solitary or occur in small clusters, measuring 6 to 25 mm in diameter. The corolla consists of five petals, which may be purple, white, or greenish-white, and are fused at their bases. The fruit is a fleshy, multi-seeded berry, 8 to 20 mm in diameter, and can be red, yellow, orange, purple, or black in color. These berries bear a resemblance to those of nightshade and bittersweet plants. In certain species, such as Lycium barbarum (commonly known as wolfberry), the fruit is edible. Most species within the Lycium genus are cosexual, meaning their flowers possess both male and female reproductive structures. However, some species exhibit sexual dimorphism, a condition where male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Research indicates that sexual dimorphism has evolved independently multiple times within the Lycium genus. Additionally, certain species, such as Lycium californicum, have populations that are both monoecious (having male and female flowers on the same plant) and dioecious (having male and female flowers on separate plants). The medicinal properties of Lycium have been recognized since ancient times. European herbalists were familiar with the plant, and it was described by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia as a treatment for sore eyes and inflammation. Similarly, Pedanius Dioscorides mentioned its medicinal uses in his work De Materia Medica. In 1753, Carl Linnaeus documented three species of Lycium—L. afrum, L. barbarum, and L. europaeum—in his publication Species Plantarum. The fruit, leaves, and bark of certain Lycium species have been utilized in China for over 2,000 years. The fruit, known in Chinese as gouqizi (枸杞子) or wolfberry (Lycium barbarum), is a staple in traditional Chinese medicine. It is commonly used in herbal teas, soups, juices, and alcoholic beverages. The berries can also be consumed whole and are employed in various traditional medicinal practices, including those of Korea, Japan, and Tibet. The berries are nutritionally dense, containing essential vitamins, minerals, dietary fiber, protein, carotenoids, polyphenols, and polysaccharides, among other bioactive compounds. Additionally, certain Lycium species serve as food sources for the larvae of some Lepidoptera species, such as Coleophora vigilis, which has been recorded feeding on Lycium ferocissimum.
